topic.title: Alopecia areata-associated white hair growth can occur independent of follicular cycling
topic.abstract: Background: Studies of alopecia areata-associated white hair (AA-WH) are scarce. Objectives: To stratify and evaluate the pathophysiological behaviour of AA-WH. Methods: This large-scale retrospective study used clinical data, dermatoscopic findings and histopathological examination. Results: AA-WH was identified in 16% (n = 826/5155) of patients with AA. Incidence increased with grey hair and age, up to 44.4% (n = 79/178) in patients ≥55 years old. Risk factors for AA-WH included older onset age, higher Severity of Alopecia Tool (SALT) scores, comorbidity with vitiligo, abnormality in thyroid function/autoantibodies and positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) tests. Compared with patients without AA-WH (AA-NWH), patients with AA-WH were older in age (P < 0.05) and in age of onset of AA (P < 0.05). Clinical AA-WH patterns could be mosaic or uniformly white; localized, diffuse and hairline distribution patterns were identified. Mosaic presentations predominated across all AA clinical subtypes, except for alopecia totalis/universalis (AT/AU). The diffuse uniform AA-WH subtype was associated with elevated total IgE (tIgE) and the presence of dust-mite-specific IgE in males ≤ 14 years old, and with abnormal thyroid function and autoantibodies, and positive ANA in females ≥36 years old (all P values < 0.05). Patients with AA-WH in their hairline or borderline of a patchy lesion tended to exhibit elevated tIgE and interleukin-4 (P values < 0.05). Compared with AA-NWH, AA-WH showed more frequent hair root depigmentation, trichomalacia, follicular pigment casts, regrowth of white vellus hair and weakly pigmented hair bulbs (all P values < 0.05). Three mechanisms are proposed for AA-WH: white vellus hair growth, transformation of pigmented terminal hair or persistence of grey hair. In situ depigmentation of pigmented terminal hairs could be observed. In patients with AA-WH with follow-up, most (81.7%, n = 353/432) recovered following treatment. Conclusions: AA-WH correlates with ageing, grey hair and autoimmunity across all age groups and allergy in juveniles. Hairline AA-WH correlates with elevated T helper 2-cytokine activity. Depigmentation of hair roots and growth of white vellus hairs contribute to AA-WH. Both depigmentation and repigmentation of hairs were observed without evidence of follicular cycling.
